routes.description: Establish that human beings possess a limited but genuine volitional capacity to regulate conscious attention, activate reason, and thereby influence deliberation and action without claiming unrestricted control over mental content, circumstances, or outcomes.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if regulating awareness is directly supportable as an agent-caused, non-necessitated capacity that changes deliberative engagement and cannot be exhaustively redescribed as compelled inference, strongest-desire operation, randomness, or mechanical event causation.

motionBridge.description: Show that voluntary regulation of conscious focus and rational engagement constitutes free will under the motion's volitional-capacity alternative.

centralBridges.description: Precisely distinguish choosing the degree and method of conscious engagement from choosing every thought, desire, conclusion, action, or outcome.
Explain how a person can cause a choice to focus without that choice being necessitated by prior events or reduced to a causeless random occurrence.
Ground the claimed capacity in awareness of modulating attention, including the ability to sustain focus, broaden context, or evade recognized considerations.
Connect chosen cognitive engagement to changes in deliberation, value ordering, operative desires, and consequent conduct.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support a conception of consciousness and causation broad enough to permit volitional agency rather than assuming an exclusively mechanical model.
Account for coercion, bodily processes, unchosen emotions, and environmental limits while preserving the narrower claimed control over awareness.

routes.description: Deny both ultimate control and the proposed capacity to activate reason by showing that actions, attention, desires, and convictions arise through determining influences or indeterminacy, neither of which makes the person the controlling author.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the proposed act of focusing remains unexplained outside determination or randomness, while introspection, deliberation, evasion, regret, and coercive choice can be accounted for without an independent volitional power.

motionBridge.description: Show that neither ultimate authorship nor voluntary control of rational focus survives the alternatives of causal determination and indeterminacy.

centralBridges.description: Apply the determined-or-random dilemma to actions and mental events, including the purported agent-caused decision to activate awareness.
Explain attention, arising considerations, rational conviction, and action through unchosen influences rather than proactive selection by a chooser.
Account for conduct, evasion, self-modification, and value-sensitive deliberation through first-order and higher-order desires whose operative strength is not freely chosen.
Establish that an immediate experience of agency does not by itself settle whether the apparent control is genuine or instead admits an alternative explanation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test libertarian control by asking what could explain divergent choices under otherwise identical relevant conditions.
Keep the conceptual objection applicable whether consciousness is characterized as material, immaterial, or emergent.

sections.title: The Scope and Locus of the Claimed Freedom
sections.rationale: The motion permits either ultimate control or a volitional capacity, making the definition of freedom and the distinction between control of attention, mental content, action, and outcome foundational to both burdens.

sections.title: Causation, Randomness, and Agent Authorship
sections.rationale: The central metaphysical clash concerns whether determination and indeterminacy exhaust the possibilities or whether an agent can cause a non-necessitated choice without converting it into randomness.

sections.title: Introspection, Experience, and Evidence of Control
sections.rationale: The positive case relies substantially on awareness of changing one's mental engagement, while the skeptical burden requires explaining why that experience may not establish the interpretation of genuine control.

sections.title: Reason, Desire, and the Mechanics of Deliberation
sections.rationale: Whether focus can be voluntarily activated and alter value-sensitive conduct, or whether considerations, convictions, and strongest desires govern the entire process, directly determines the viability of the motion's narrower alternative.

sections.title: Consciousness, Constraints, and Applied Choice
sections.rationale: Accounts of mind, coercion, bodily limits, emotion formation, regret, and evasion test whether the competing causal models remain coherent when applied beyond abstract choice examples.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Neither causal determination nor indeterminacy permits a person to be the ultimate author or controller of an action.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening turn is explicitly assigned to Alex and consistently presents the free-will-skeptical position.

response.rationale: Constructively presents the skeptic's principal determined-or-random route against controlling authorship.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly develops the motion-level skeptical case rather than addressing an earlier opposing move.

precisionFindings.rationale: The dilemma and ultimate-authorship conclusion are recoverable, though control and ultimate cause receive only compressed specification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical dilemma is intelligible, but exhaustiveness and the move from external causal ancestry to absent control remain compressed.

charity.alternative: A person might exercise nonultimate but genuine control within a causal history originating partly outside the person.
charity.decisiveQualification: The stated argument targets ultimate authorship more clearly than every narrower form of volitional control.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is coherent but leaves material bridges concerning exhaustive alternatives and why causal ancestry eliminates relevant control.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The bottle example illustrates the claim, but the exhaustiveness and control warrants receive little independent defense.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This directly advances the skeptic's motion-level requirement of denying controlling authorship.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes common compatibilist distinctions nearby, but its selected inference only partially accommodates narrower agency.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly contrasts randomness with a causal chain extending beyond the self and infers that an externally originating chain defeats ultimate authorship.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Causation does not entail necessitation by prior events, so treating every caused occurrence as predetermined improperly collapses two distinct concepts.
moves.attributionBasis: This passage remains within Craig's uninterrupted opening turn and directly characterizes Alex's use of the term determined.

components.text: Challenges the premise that being caused entails being necessitated or predetermined by prior events.
Does not yet explain how non-necessitated causation supplies control rather than indeterminacy.

response.rationale: It contacts the dilemma's determination premise but does not complete the positive account needed to defeat the randomness horn.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a substantial partial answer because it contacts a decisive premise while leaving the rival horn unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between causation and necessitation is stated plainly and without material scope drift.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The distinction is defensible, but asserting that all events are caused and not all necessitated receives no supporting account here.

charity.alternative: The skeptic may use determined to include sufficiently caused rather than strictly necessitated events.
charity.decisiveQualification: The skeptic's control dilemma can survive the verbal distinction unless non-necessitated causation is explained.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conceptual distinction is valid, but the conclusion that the dilemma improperly collapses categories needs a fuller account of determination.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies on conceptual assertion and supplies no representative case or defended account of caused but non-necessitated choice.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central exhaustive-dilemma bridge by separating causation from necessitation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response identifies a real ambiguity but treats it as more dispositive than the strongest skeptical formulation permits.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly says everything happening is caused while denying that everything is necessitated by prior events.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: People can introspectively observe themselves regulating mental effort and choosing whether to activate reason, drift, or evade, evidencing the relevant volitional capacity.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig retains the floor throughout and identifies the capacity to activate the mind as his account of free will.

components.text: Offers introspective observation of choosing mental activation as evidence for controlled agency.
Does not explain why the observed choice escapes both determination and indeterminacy.

response.rationale: The move supplies issue-bearing experiential evidence but only partially answers the causal dilemma's explanatory demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts control through alleged observation, while leaving the decisive causal classification substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed capacity is recoverable, but activate reason, drift, and evade are not sharply operationalized or bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Introspective awareness may support apparent regulation, but it does not by itself establish the asserted causal interpretation.

charity.alternative: Introspection may reveal changes in effort while remaining neutral about whether their causes are voluntarily authored.
charity.decisiveQualification: The experiential datum and the libertarian interpretation require separate warrants.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from experienced regulation to the relevant volitional capacity leaves a material interpretation bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The city exercise and introspective appeal are concrete, but they are not independently verified and rival explanations are not compared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable evidence-of-awareness bridge through claimed observation of regulating focus.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents the experience clearly but substantially compresses the strongest alternative interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks listeners to observe that they choose whether to activate their minds, use reason, drift, or evade.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Free will is the capacity to activate and use the rational faculty, rather than a power to select every mental content, action, or outcome.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker remains Craig, who develops his announced broad account of rational and emotional faculties without interruption.

components.text: Reframes the motion-relevant freedom as activating rational engagement rather than ultimate authorship of every outcome.
Preserves the control issue by locating it in whether the rational faculty is voluntarily activated.

response.rationale: The motion expressly permits a volitional-capacity alternative, so replacing ultimate authorship with controlled rational activation is justified.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reframe preserves the legitimate control question and clearly identifies the narrower capacity being defended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The narrower locus is explicit, though activate reason and use the mind remain somewhat underspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The definition is clear, but claiming rational faculty and free will necessarily arrive together exceeds the support supplied.

charity.alternative: A rational faculty might operate through causally produced attention without a separate voluntary activation power.
charity.decisiveQualification: Defining the locus of freedom does not establish that the proposed activating capacity exists.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The scope distinction is useful, but the claim that an unusable faculty is no faculty and therefore free will exists is insufficiently bridged.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The passage mainly asserts a functional definition and necessity relation without evidence distinguishing voluntary from caused activation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion's explicit volitional-capacity alternative by defining free will as rational activation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The narrower formulation is fair and relevant, but it does not engage the strongest causal alternative to that formulation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies free will with the capacity to activate reason or use the mind, rather than selection of every mental content.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: A person can consider broader values and originate a choice caused by the agent without that choice being random or necessitated by prior factors.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig continues the same turn, applies his account to desires, and concludes expressly with agent causation before Alex resumes.

components.text: Answers the dilemma by positing the agent as the cause of a choice that is neither causeless nor prior-event necessitated.
Does not provide a mechanism or criterion distinguishing agent causation from unexplained indeterminacy.

response.rationale: The reply explicitly addresses both horns but leaves the skeptic's central explanatory challenge materially underdeveloped.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts both stated horns, yet the answer remains compressed at exactly the disputed explanatory point.

precisionFindings.rationale: Agent as primary cause is recoverable, but agent causation is not defined beyond denying prior necessitation and causelessness.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The confident primary-cause conclusion is asserted without enough warrant to exclude determined or random redescriptions.

charity.alternative: Calling the person the cause may redescribe the event without explaining why the causal occurrence was controlled.
charity.decisiveQualification: A successful agent-causal reply must distinguish origination from both event determination and chance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposed third category is internally intelligible but risks stipulation because its distinguishing causal conditions are not supplied.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The central metaphysical claim rests primarily on assertion, with no defended example or independent support for primary agent causation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It squarely addresses the indispensable agent-causation bridge and the skeptic's causal dilemma.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move directly denies both skeptical categories but omits the strongest demand for a differentiating explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls the person the primary cause and says the choice is caused by the agent without being necessitated by prior factors.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: The felt immediacy of an experience cannot establish its interpretation, because introspection can present illusory forces or agencies as real.
moves.attributionBasis: Alex explicitly takes the floor after Craig's opening and directly discusses Craig's perceptual and introspective methodology.

components.text: Identifies the inference from felt immediacy to the truth of its causal interpretation as invalid.
Does not independently resolve whether agent causation is coherent.

response.rationale: The centrifugal-force analogy diagnoses why the experiential premise cannot alone establish genuine volitional control.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly isolates the decisive evidential inference and states the defeating consequence for introspective proof.

precisionFindings.rationale: The modest conclusion that introspection alone is insufficient is precise and consistently bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The force matches the analogy-supported conclusion and is carefully limited to insufficiency rather than universal unreliability.

charity.alternative: The defender may claim direct awareness of choosing, not merely a feeling interpreted through theory.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even direct-seeming awareness does not automatically settle the causal status of the observed event.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogy supports the limited inference that phenomenological certainty does not entail interpretive correctness, with only a bounded analogy gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The centrifugal-force example is specific and apt, though it does not demonstrate that volitional experience is actually illusory.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro side's central evidence-awareness bridge by defeating introspection as sufficient proof.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly preserves the experiential datum while challenging only the stronger interpretation drawn from it.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt compares introspective certainty with feeling an illusory centrifugal force and concludes that seeming true is insufficient.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Attention to deliberation reveals thoughts, options, and rational conclusions presenting themselves rather than being proactively selected by a chooser.
moves.attributionBasis: Alex remains the sole speaker and explicitly reexamines Craig's city example and the Objectivist account of activating reason.

components.text: Examines the city exercise and argues that candidate thoughts arise without proactive selection.
Does not fully address the narrower claim that method or degree of attention, rather than content, is chosen.

response.rationale: It answers the content-selection implication of the example but only partially contacts the defender's distinct focus-regulation claim.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply is a strong partial answer because it tests the example while leaving the method-versus-content distinction open.

precisionFindings.rationale: Unselected arising content is clear, but the move sometimes ranges from content to deliberation generally without explicit separation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The introspective invitation appropriately supports a defeasible claim about content arising rather than a categorical neurological conclusion.

charity.alternative: The defender concedes unbidden content while locating freedom in how consciously to engage with that content.
charity.decisiveQualification: Unchosen content alone does not disprove voluntary regulation of method or sustained focus.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The city example coherently supports unchosen content, though extending that result to absence of a chooser needs another bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The common introspective exercise is representative but lacks verification and does not discriminate fully among accounts of attention.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central deliberative-compulsion bridge by locating arising options outside proactive selection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply identifies a genuine limit on choice but incompletely handles the strongest narrower account already presented.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt revisits the city example and asks whether the participant chose which city would arise in awareness.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Agent causation does not end the explanatory regress, because conscious actions follow unchosen desires and the strongest operative desire governs behavior.
moves.attributionBasis: Alex continues uninterrupted, names Craig's agent-causation claim, and develops the desire argument through several connected examples.

components.text: Challenges agent authorship by tracing conscious action to desires whose existence and operative strength are unchosen.
Does not exclude the possibility that chosen rational engagement alters which desire becomes operative.

response.rationale: The desire account contacts the authorship claim directly but leaves the proposed role of focus in modifying deliberation unresolved.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It addresses a decisive explanatory component with developed examples while leaving a material pro-side qualification open.

precisionFindings.rationale: The desire-governed account is recoverable, but strongest desire shifts between immediate want and all-things-considered motivation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The gym example supports broader motivational competition, but universal governance by the strongest desire is partly definitional.

charity.alternative: Agents may form higher-order commitments and alter motivation through reflective practices over time.
charity.decisiveQualification: The skeptic must show those reflective processes are themselves wholly governed by unchosen operative desires.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The regress from action to operative desire is coherent, though defining the victorious motive as strongest risks circularity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several familiar examples illustrate motivational conflict, but the universal explanatory conclusion lacks independent comparative support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central desire-account bridge and challenges the claimed practical influence of chosen focus.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument anticipates apparent counterexamples but compresses the strongest diachronic self-shaping alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt uses the gym case to argue that apparent action against desire reflects another stronger desire or valued benefit.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Free will selects the method of conscious engagement rather than subconscious content, allowing chosen rational focus to affect which desire ultimately governs action.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator-like transition at event 864 is followed by Biddle answering Alex by name and presenting the pro-side account continuously.

components.text: Explains that unbidden subconscious content does not answer the distinct claim that conscious method is chosen.
Claims chosen method can affect the governing desire but does not fully explain that causal influence.

response.rationale: The response diagnoses a content-versus-method mismatch and states why unchosen thoughts do not by themselves defeat regulated engagement.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive inference and preserves the legitimate question at the level of conscious method.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conscious-method and subconscious-content distinction is stated consistently and with a clear scope boundary.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The distinction is well supported by the example, but the further claim of voluntary method selection remains incompletely warranted.

charity.alternative: Although content is unbidden, the selected method of engagement might also arise through unchosen causes.
charity.decisiveQualification: Separating content from method does not itself establish freedom at the method level.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction successfully blocks one overextension, with a bounded missing bridge from distinct method to voluntarily controlled method.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Humpty Dumpty example clearly supports unbidden content, but evidence for freely chosen method remains largely introspective.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central deliberative-compulsion claim and supports the central definition of focus.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately corrects the content objection but gives limited attention to the strongest causal challenge to method choice.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes conscious awareness from subconscious material that appears unbidden and locates free will in choice of method.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Agent causation does not explain control because a mental event either has determining causes beyond the agent's ultimate control or occurs causelessly and randomly.
moves.attributionBasis: After the topic is identified as agent causation, O'Connor develops the leaf, wind, brain, and materialist cases until Biddle begins his response.

components.text: Applies the caused-or-causeless dilemma directly to the alleged agent-caused mental event.
Treats caused events as falling under determining causes without fully answering the cause-versus-necessitation distinction.
Extends the dilemma to mental method choice but does not separately analyze attentional regulation.

response.rationale: The reply squarely addresses agent causation, although its determining-cause horn needs a more exact answer to non-necessitating causation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the central agent-causal claim and both proposed alternatives, with one material conceptual bridge compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The event dilemma is clear, but caused, determined, and beyond control are linked without consistently distinct definitions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The dilemma has substantial conceptual force, but its exhaustiveness and equation of cause with determination remain underqualified.

charity.alternative: Agent causation proposes a caused event whose source is the continuing person rather than a sufficient prior event.
charity.decisiveQualification: The skeptic must show that this proposal is incoherent or collapses into one horn, not merely restate the horns.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The dichotomy is lucid, but the caused horn relies on an insufficiently defended transition from having causes to absent control.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Materialist mental events provide a concrete application, though the conclusion is primarily conceptual and rival causal models remain underexamined.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro side's indispensable agent-causation bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move targets the proposal directly but only partially explains why agent causation cannot constitute a third causal category.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt classifies mental events as happenings that either lack causes and are random or have causes outside ultimate control.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Human consciousness is a real nonphysical existent whose rational faculty operates by choice, making a purely material and mechanistic account of human agency incomplete.
moves.attributionBasis: Biddle announces that he is not a materialist and then gives a continuous first-person account of consciousness, mind, and chosen reason.

components.text: Asserts a nonphysical mind but does not show why its choices escape the caused-or-causeless dilemma.
Provides contrary metaphysical material without answering the dilemma's theory-independent structure.

response.rationale: Rejecting materialism is relevant background, but the decisive causal classification applies to nonphysical events unless separately defeated.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is relevant contrary material rather than an answer to the causal dilemma's decisive demand.

precisionFindings.rationale: Body, mind, and rational faculty are distinguishable, but nonphysical existent and operates by choice lack further specification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The existence and choice-governed operation of a nonphysical mind are asserted more strongly than the passage's warrants support.

charity.alternative: The skeptic's dilemma may apply to immaterial mental events just as it applies to physical events.
charity.decisiveQualification: Ontological nonmechanism does not by itself establish controlled, nonrandom origination.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The dual-aspect ontology is not self-contradictory, but its asserted connection to choice does not answer the causal inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The claims about nonphysical consciousness and choice rest predominantly on assertion without alternative comparison or specific support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the subsidiary causal-pluralism bridge but does not reach the central causal challenge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply largely substitutes a metaphysical assertion for engagement with the strongest theory-independent objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes humans as physical bodies with nonphysical minds and says the human rational faculty operates by choice.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Although present emotions are not directly chosen, repeated choices to think can revise value judgments and thereby shape emotional dispositions and operative desires over time.
moves.attributionBasis: Biddle explicitly corrects Alex's characterization of his view on desires and develops the distinction between immediate feeling and long-term formation.

components.text: Answers the fixed-desire picture by arguing that repeated reasoning revises value judgments and later emotions.
Does not establish that the earlier choices to reason were themselves freely selected.
Does not resolve the causal status of the self-shaping choices.

response.rationale: The diachronic account contacts the strongest-desire claim but leaves the regress concerning the origin of reflective choices unresolved.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies a developed partial answer about changing desires while leaving the causal authorship demand unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between immediate emotional control and gradual value formation is explicit and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The temporal qualification is careful, though ultimate control over values exceeds what the described revision process alone establishes.

charity.alternative: Value revision over time may itself be fully produced by prior desires, evidence, and circumstances.
charity.decisiveQualification: Self-modification supports practical influence without yet proving non-determined authorship.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The diachronic mechanism is coherent, with one material missing bridge from reflective revision to freely authored revision.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The account is psychologically plausible and qualified but remains general and lacks representative evidence or rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central desire account and supports practical influence through value-sensitive deliberation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly concedes immediate limits but does not fully confront the strongest causal interpretation of long-term change.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt concedes no direct immediate control of emotion while claiming corrected thinking can change value judgments and feelings over time.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: The observable capacity to evade recognized facts shows that rational evidence does not compel acceptance and supplies direct introspective evidence of free will.
moves.attributionBasis: Biddle frames the passage as an answer to Alex's claim about rational compulsion and continuously presents evasion and introspection as pro-side evidence.

components.text: Argues that a person can evade recognized considerations rather than being compelled by rational content.
Reasserts direct introspective evidence without answering why its causal interpretation might be mistaken.
Does not explain whether evasion is determined, agent-caused, or indeterminate.

response.rationale: Observable evasion contacts rational compulsion but does not defeat the earlier interpretation and causal challenges.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts one decisive deliberative component while leaving two central skeptical objections substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: Evasion is recognizable, but observation, direct evidence, self-evidence, and proof are used with insufficiently stable evidential scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that observable evasion proves free will greatly exceeds evidence that people sometimes reject recognized considerations.

charity.alternative: Evasion may be conscious and reason-resistant while still arising from stronger desires or determining causes.
charity.decisiveQualification: Failure to follow evidence establishes noncompulsion by that evidence, not independent volitional authorship.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from capacity to evade to proof of free will is a substantial non sequitur without a causal exclusion argument.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Evasion is an observable phenomenon, but the move supplies no evidence discriminating free agency from motivated or determined avoidance.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central awareness-evidence bridge through the claimed observable regulation of engagement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move omits the strongest desire-based and causal explanations and treats the behavioral datum as decisive proof.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls the capacity to evade direct, self-evident proof of free will because a person can observe evasion.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Libertarian free will requires a genuine ability to act differently in physically identical circumstances, for which no differentiating explanation is available.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor explicitly states his definition and directs the resulting identical-worlds challenge to Craig by name.

response.rationale: Constructively states an alternate-possibilities test involving divergent action under otherwise identical physical circumstances.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly develops a material subsidiary skeptical test without purporting to answer an earlier move.

precisionFindings.rationale: The possible-world test is recoverable, though physically identical and relevantly identical are not fully distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The challenge is appropriately interrogative, but treating alternate possibilities as the required conception needs further defense.

charity.alternative: The motion also permits a narrower volitional capacity that need not require divergent action in an exactly duplicated world.
charity.decisiveQualification: The identical-world test bears most directly on libertarian alternate possibilities, not every proposed focus capacity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The differentiating-explanation challenge is coherent, though its applicability depends on a contested definition of the relevant freedom.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The possible-world construction clarifies the conceptual demand but supplies no independent warrant that this condition is necessary.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the subsidiary alternate-possibilities bridge rather than the entire motion-level skeptical route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move articulates a strong libertarian test but incompletely accommodates the motion's explicitly narrower alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks what could differentiate choices in two universes stipulated to be exactly alike and associates freedom with acting otherwise.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Introspective confidence in free will is defeasible when philosophical considerations provide alternative explanations of the apparent experience.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer is explicitly addressed to Alex and the responding speaker clarifies his own earlier analogy and skeptical argument.

components.text: Reiterates that introspection alone cannot establish free will when a philosophical defeater is available.
Preserves ordinary experiential trust while denying that it resolves the special causal question.
Does not depend on rejecting the defender's account of consciousness.

response.rationale: The response directly answers renewed appeals to self-evidence by distinguishing ordinary experience from contested philosophical interpretation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive evidential claim and states the limited defeating consequence with appropriate scope.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is carefully limited to introspection's insufficiency when a relevant alternative explanation exists.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The qualified skepticism matches the available warrant and expressly avoids global distrust of sense experience.

charity.alternative: Direct awareness of regulating attention may have stronger prima facie standing than an ordinary inference from sensation.
charity.decisiveQualification: A targeted causal argument can still defeat confidence in the libertarian interpretation without denying the experience.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between trusting ordinary experience and withholding a contested causal interpretation is explicit and consistent.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The response supplies a clear epistemic comparison, though it depends on the independent strength of the philosophical defeater.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro side's central evidence-awareness bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately preserves the strongest experiential claim while explaining its limited epistemic reach.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly says introspection alone is insufficient while denying that this entails general distrust of experience or sense data.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: The alternate-possibilities conception of free will is philosophically incoherent regardless of whether consciousness is material, immaterial, or emergent.
moves.attributionBasis: The question is directed into the debate and O'Connor identifies his own anti-free-will argument while distinguishing it from scientific approaches.

components.text: States that the anti-free-will argument does not depend on materialism and therefore survives a nonphysical mind.
Does not independently demonstrate that agent causation is incoherent under every theory of consciousness.
Does not separately analyze whether a theory-neutral focus capacity is coherent.

response.rationale: It directly neutralizes the materialism objection but does not by itself complete the claimed theory-independent incoherence proof.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the ontology-dependent reply while leaving the underlying causal demonstration materially compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: Theory independence is clear, but the stronger proposition of incoherence is not fully recoverable from the selected discussion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Ambivalence about consciousness theory is supported, but complete philosophical incoherence is asserted beyond the passage's shown reasoning.

charity.alternative: A nonphysical agent-causal theory might supply causal categories unavailable to reductive materialism.
charity.decisiveQualification: Theory independence requires explaining why the same control dilemma applies to such categories.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The theory-neutral strategy is coherent, but the bridge from neutrality to incoherence is materially underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The passage supports neutrality toward materialism but offers limited specific support for the broader impossibility conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the subsidiary causal-pluralism bridge and supports the skeptic's theory-independence requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges suspicion of materialism but only briefly handles the strongest nonphysical agent-causal alternative.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: External force can sharply restrict available actions and obstruct a person's exercise of rational judgment and free will without disproving the underlying volitional capacity.
moves.attributionBasis: Biddle explicitly takes the first response and develops the answer using his established account of rational faculty and volitional choice.

components.text: Reframes coercion as limiting the exercise and available outputs of a capacity rather than eliminating the capacity itself.
Does not answer the general causal incoherence argument.
Does not establish that the remaining judgment under coercion escapes desire governance.

response.rationale: The distinction between possessing and successfully exercising a capacity legitimately preserves the applied control issue under coercion.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reframe clearly answers the applied constraint question, though it does not resolve the deeper causal objections.

precisionFindings.rationale: External limits, available actions, and exercise of rational choice are clearly distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move makes a bounded claim about impeded exercise and does not infer unrestricted freedom under coercion.

charity.alternative: Coercion can leave conscious selection between options while drastically changing incentives and ordinary responsibility.
charity.decisiveQualification: Remaining selection does not itself settle whether the underlying process is libertarian or determined.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The possession-versus-exercise distinction coherently accommodates external force with one bounded unresolved causal issue.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The coercion application is concrete and plausible, though the moral characterization adds little evidential support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary scope-constraints bridge rather than establishing the motion-level capacity.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly distinguishes constraint from capacity, with only the deeper causal qualification omitted.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says physical force limits choices and prevents people from using rational judgment and free will in directing their lives.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: The fundamental volitional choice is whether and how fully to activate one's mind, with degrees ranging from full-context awareness to evasion or drift.
moves.attributionBasis: The same identified respondent marks a conceptual pivot and restates the distinctive focus-versus-evasion account he has defended throughout the exchange.

components.text: Specifies the relevant alternatives as degrees and methods of mental activation rather than arbitrary content selection.
Directly preserves unbidden content while locating the claimed choice in full-context engagement, drift, or evasion.
Does not explain how graded activation escapes the theory-independent causal dilemma.

response.rationale: The move clarifies the locus and gradation of alternatives but does not answer what causally differentiates those degrees.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the definitional and content objections while leaving the decisive causal qualification unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The nonbinary range from full-context thinking through degrees of evasion and drift is clearly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The graded model is carefully qualified, though calling each degree a fundamental choice remains insufficiently warranted.

charity.alternative: Degrees of attention may vary continuously because of fatigue, salience, habit, or desire rather than voluntary selection.
charity.decisiveQualification: A precise scale of engagement does not establish agent control over position on that scale.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The graded scope account is internally coherent, with a material remaining bridge from degree of activation to choice.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The distinctions fit ordinary experience but lack specific support discriminating voluntary regulation from causal variation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central define-focus bridge by specifying the degrees and locus of the claimed freedom.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move handles binary and content objections well but gives limited attention to nonvolitional sources of graded attention.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says the fundamental choice concerns activating the mind and describes a continuum from full-context thought to evasion or drift.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Even conscious conduct under coercion remains technically a choice between desire-governed alternatives, although ordinary language reasonably describes it as forced.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor identifies his own preferred terminology, develops the wallet-at-gunpoint example, and connects it to his earlier desire-based skeptical framework.

components.text: Agrees that coercion restricts meaningful options while maintaining that conscious surrender remains technically a choice.
Does not determine whether the conscious selection or its degree of engagement is freely authored.

response.rationale: The reply directly addresses the coercion application and reconciles philosophical choice language with ordinary descriptions of force.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It fully contacts the applied coercion claim, while appropriately leaving the broader metaphysical dispute separate.

precisionFindings.rationale: Technical choice, conscious action, ordinary forced language, and restricted alternatives are carefully distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker explicitly qualifies the technical terminology and acknowledges exceptional choices under coercion.

charity.alternative: The defender uses free choice to denote uncoerced exercise, not the mere presence of conscious alternatives.
charity.decisiveQualification: Calling coerced surrender a technical choice does not establish freedom in the defender's stronger sense.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between conscious selection and ordinary forced action is explicit, consistent, and handles the apparent counterexample.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The wallet-at-gunpoint example is concrete and representative, though it supports terminology more than the general desire theory.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the subsidiary scope-constraints account without independently completing the skeptic's central route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly recognizes the ordinary and philosophical senses and does not pretend the terminological agreement resolves metaphysics.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt treats handing over a wallet at gunpoint as technically a conscious choice while accepting ordinary language that it was forced.
